parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist begins the morning angry with his boy for oversleeping and forgetting his lute, then works at his office before visiting Gresham College. There he takes pleasure in hearing Commissioner Pett expertly dominate a shipbuilding discussion with Mr. Castle, appreciating both Pett's extraordinary ability and Lord Brunker's mastery. Though he finds it difficult to make himself return to work, late at the office he does business to his content. That evening he receives sad news that two of their ships have been lost by running aground in the Straits, with more nearly lost, and a Dutch fleet heading toward their lame ships. Upon coming home at night he is much troubled to learn that his poor canary bird, kept for three or four years, is dead.
parsed.narrative.meaning: His pleasure in witnessing expert discourse affirms the value he places on mastery and competence in shipbuilding matters. The loss of two ships, with the danger of further losses to the Dutch fleet, leads him to call the news most sad and to ask God to make them mindful of it. The small loss of his long-kept canary bird troubles him profoundly at the close of the day.

He prays for God's preservation and pardon, then goes home to dinner, works at the office until late, and retires to bed.

After landing her again, Pepys went about his day, dining with Creed and Povy and visiting Lord Bellasses and the Duke of Albemarle. He then spoke at length with Mr. Slingsby about the Mint and coinage, hearing arguments that the law prohibiting bullion export is a folly. He ended the day at his office, busy late, then home to supper and bed.
parsed.narrative.meaning: The maid's choice to follow her fortune with an unworthy man, even foreseeing her own ruin, struck Pepys as a strange, stupid thing.

Returning home, he was drawn into a household dispute over a servant's conduct, which escalated into high words with his wife. He resolved to dismiss the servant and to take a course with the boy involved, fearing he had spoiled him. Later, to ease his mind, he discharged himself of a sum of money by making himself debtor to Mr. Povy, accepting the loss for the sake of a quiet mind. He stayed up working on his accounts until almost two in the morning, reflecting that his worth had come down to L1257 for the month and praising God for what he had.

parsed.narrative.summary: Samuel Pepys is vexed by being continually put upon uncertain and servile business about getting ships for Tangier. After dinner and office work, his wife calls him home over a dispute with Jane; he hears both sides, finds his wife much at fault for favouring Tom, and has high words with her, deciding the wench shall go and that he will take a course with the boy. To ease his mind he makes himself debtor to Mr. Povy for L117 5s. gained the previous month, preferring a quiet mind and certainty over the sum. He works on his accounts until almost two in the morning and gives thanks for what he has, now down to L1257.
parsed.narrative.meaning: A quiet mind and certainty of one's own is worth more than a sum of money that may bring trouble and questions.

parsed.narrative.summary: The narrator records an ordinary busy day at the office, interrupted by a serious conversation with his son's lute-master, whom he threatens to dismiss unless the boy improves. The next day, he takes his wife to Whitehall Chapel, briefly visits a tavern, and hears a celebrated young preacher deliver a sermon that impresses him deeply as the best he has ever heard. Afterwards they dine at Mr. Povy's, where the host's excessive praise is distasteful to him, and then ride out into the fields before returning home. The evening is spent with friends making music, during which a musical argument grows heated but ends amicably, and the narrator laughs about it later with Creed before they go to bed.
parsed.narrative.meaning: Faithful preaching and good music matter deeply, while excessive self-praise is repellent.

Afterwards he takes coach with 'the fairest flower' to Tothill Fields for air, eats cake and enjoys intimate liberties with her, then parts without notice. Returning home, he notes that by pleasure he was made to forget everything, and that the coachman and people at the house cannot know him again; late, news comes that the fleet is in sight of the Dutch ships.
parsed.narrative.meaning: The pleasure of the evening made him forget everything that is, and the arrangements let him slip away unnoticed so that the coachman and the people at the house cannot know him again.

salience.tether.stake: pleasure and secrecy

canon.narrative.summary: The narrator wakes before four with pain in urinating, attributing it to drinking too much cold drink the night before. After returning to sleep and going to the office, he dines with Sir G. Carteret and the Board, where they make mirth of a poorly written letter from Sir W. Batten with news of the fleet. He then feels great vexation that nothing has been done by the Controller to right the King in Sir G. Carteret's accounts, writes letters all afternoon, and in the evening visits Sir Ph. Warwicke about Tangier money. He calls on Lady Sandwich, who waits hourly for news of her husband but remains, he observes, in the best temper he has ever seen, neither confident nor troubled with fear. She tells him of developments regarding Mrs. Mallett and Lord Hinchingbroke, after which he returns to his office and then home to bed before midnight.

Throughout the day his mind is ill at ease because no news has come of the fleet and Lord Sandwich, with ill reports running about of Sandwich being killed. He waits at White Hall and at home until midnight for news and for his wife's return, then goes to bed. On Drury Lane he sees houses marked with red crosses and 'Lord have mercy upon us,' the first plague-marked houses he remembers seeing, which saddens him. The sight makes him buy roll-tobacco to smell and chew, which removes his apprehension.
canon.narrative.meaning: The first sight of plague-marked houses gave him an ill conception of himself and his smell, which tobacco could take away.

parsed.narrative.summary: The narrator wakes early feeling full of fear of an ague but resolves to go out anyway, wrapping up warm and travelling by water to the Tower, where he reads the weekly bill and sees that 8,252 have died, including 6,878 of the plague, which he calls a most dreadful number. He then journeys to Brainford reading a play, is met by Mr. Povy, and they travel merrily together to Sir R. Viner's pleasant house at Swakely. There he is shown the house and grounds with great respect, including a screen with portraits, marble fixtures, and a preserved black boy who died of consumption and was dried in an oven. After a dinner with fine company and songs by Mrs. Worship, he concludes his business to his content about getting a promise of money, and he and Povy have a most pleasant journey back with much discourse about Court persons. He learns the King is not well and out of humour, possibly in a consumption, and is weary of everything. He returns by boat to Woolwich around one in the morning, finding his wife and all in bed.
parsed.narrative.meaning: Even amid the plague's dreadful hold, the journey yields pleasure, good company, and successful business that outweigh the early fear.

salience.tether.stake: the plague continuing among us

Howe used his name in shipping goods under false pretense, which vexes him mightily, though he says little until he can speak with Lord Bruncker. He ends the evening playing cards with young women at his lodgings.

parsed.narrative.summary: The narrator spends the morning on administrative business, recommending a clerk to Sir J. Minnes and thereby ridding himself of someone he feared would not suit his purposes. At noon he dines merrily with Mr. Hill and Mr. Houbland and their brothers, then is called away to negotiate tallys with Mr. Andrews, clearing £210 to himself. In the evening he watches Lord Bruncker dismantle and reassemble a watch, an experience he finds immensely instructive, and he later talks with his lordship until late at night. He is vexed by Madam Williams's snappish reply to his jest, and by the Duke of Albemarle's letter insisting that meetings continue over Christmas. The entry closes with him catching up his journal, his mind eased, and with frosty weather prompting hope that the plague will abate, otherwise it will certainly continue into the next year.
parsed.narrative.meaning: The narrator views the successful negotiation to clear £210 as a welcome addition to his late profits, which he has resolved to settle precisely before attending to the Duke of Albemarle.
